title: Qatar Tells Europe to Wait Until 2027 and Pakistan Pays Double for the Gas It Used to Get on Contract
subhead: QatarEnergy has extended force majeure on LNG deliveries to Italy's Edison and to South Asian buyers to the end of December, pushing TTF to $108.51/MWh — its highest since 2022 — and forcing Pakistan to fund a billion-dollar spot bill. Gas, not crude, is now where this war bites hardest.

sections.heading: QatarEnergy Freezes Europe Out Until January
sections.body:
QatarEnergy has extended its force majeure on LNG deliveries to the end of December 2026, according to notices received by Italian utility Edison and confirmed to Reuters by a source at Bangladesh's Petrobangla. Edison, one of QatarEnergy's largest European long-term buyers, was told it would not receive three further cargoes at the Adriatic LNG terminal. The force majeure has been in place since April 2026, after Iranian strikes damaged Qatar's Ras Laffan export hub.

The effect on price was immediate. The Dutch TTF front-month contract traded at $108.51/MWh (97.53 euros) on Wednesday, the highest level since the 2022 energy crisis — the first winter Europe spent without most Russian pipeline gas. Oilprice.com notes that LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz have not recovered in any meaningful way, even as Middle East crude exports have partially done so.

The scale of the loss is stark. Reuters calculated at end-August that Qatar's LNG exports had been cut by 96%, and ICIS data showed Qatar shipped just 18 cargoes through end-August against 509 in the same period of 2025.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe has spent two years buying LNG as a substitute for Russian pipelines and now finds its largest single LNG supplier effectively offline for a second winter. Storage alone will not cover this — Germany is still rushing to fill tanks, per Reuters.

sections.heading: South Asia Pays the Premium: Pakistan's Billion-Dollar Winter and Bangladesh's Cost Squeeze
sections.body:
The same force majeure lands much harder on buyers with no alternative. Petrobangla chairman Abdul Mannan told Reuters the company is 'trying to secure additional spot cargoes to bridge the supply gap, but at a significant cost, driving our import bill sharply higher and putting considerable pressure on our finances.'

Pakistan will pay more than $1 billion for winter LNG, per local daily Tribune, as it buys 10 spot cargoes for November 2026 to February 2027 at roughly double the price of its Qatari term contracts. Wood Mackenzie has called Pakistan the South Asian market most affected by the loss of Qatari supply; the country sourced 99% of its 2025 LNG imports from Qatar.

India, by contrast, is absorbing the shock through volume: imports are set to hit a record 2.8 million tonnes in October (up 18% year-on-year) even with Asian benchmarks tripling to about $33/MMBtu, per Oilprice.com. Arrivals from Qatar and the UAE are up 80% and 30% month-on-month respectively as partial Gulf flows resume.
sections.whyItMatters: The war's LNG damage is being distributed by balance-sheet strength: India buys through it, Pakistan and Bangladesh borrow through it. That is a sovereign-credit story disguised as an energy story.

sections.heading: Washington Warns Gulf Capitals to Prepare for a Second Iran Campaign After the Midterms
sections.body:
The Wall Street Journal reported that Washington has told several Gulf states to prepare for a possible renewed U.S. military campaign against Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, as cited by The National and Oilprice.com. In parallel, Qatari mediators have handed Tehran a new draft deal to end the war, with an Iranian response expected by the end of the week, according to the same reporting.

On the water, Iran's position has deteriorated faster than its rhetoric suggests. The U.S. Navy reinstated its blockade in the Gulf of Oman in mid-July after the collapse of the 'deal to make a deal,' and UANI tracking puts at least 50 laden Iranian tankers stranded inside the Gulf. Kpler data, cited by the Wall Street Journal, shows Iran's floating storage outside the blockade falling from close to 150 million barrels before April to just 866,000 barrels by mid-October, with a further 43 million barrels trapped inside the blockade zone.

Iran's Plan and Budget Organization is reportedly modelling a $130-a-barrel scenario for the budget year starting March 2027, per Fars News Agency (via Iran International) — an aspiration that would not help Tehran while its exports are near zero.
sections.whyItMatters: Two clocks are running: a diplomatic one ending this week with Iran's answer to Doha, and a military one ending after November 3. The Gulf producers know which one Washington is preparing for, and that is why they are renting storage in Singapore and discounting crude into Europe.

sections.heading: Missiles on Ras Tanura: The Attack Campaign Moves to the Export Terminal
sections.body:
Yemen's Houthis claimed a ballistic missile strike on Saudi Aramco's Ras Tanura refinery and terminal on Tuesday, saying spokesman Yahya Saree reported a fire at the complex. Saudi authorities did not confirm a direct hit; Bloomberg, citing a person familiar, reported the fire near the terminal had been contained. Ras Tanura has capacity of 550,000 barrels per day and, with Yanbu on the Red Sea, handles nearly all Saudi crude exports — both have been attacked before.

The Houthis also claimed strikes on the Saudi Ministry of Defense, Abha International Airport, two military transport aircraft at Najran, and said they repelled a Saudi-backed advance near Bab al-Mandeb. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a missile aimed at Taif. Brent traded at $115.30 and WTI at $101.90 on Wednesday after the claim.
sections.whyItMatters: Attacking a refinery is an attack on product supply and export revenue at once. Saudi Arabia's ability to keep discounting crude into Europe — the strategy it began this week — depends on terminals that are now being targeted directly.

sections.heading: The Russian Diesel Cargo Loses Its Destination, and the Blumenthal Deadline Nears
sections.body:
The Agioi Fanendes, the tanker billed as the first to carry Russian diesel to the United States under the Trump-Putin deal, has dropped New York as its destination. The Malta-flagged vessel left Primorsk on October 22 with about 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low-sulfur diesel, was reported idling off Skagen, Denmark on October 26, and now shows 'for orders', per Oilprice.com.

Senator Richard Blumenthal wrote on October 27 to the tanker's Athens-based owner, Eastern Mediterranean Maritime, demanding recall of the vessel and disclosure of seller, buyer, charterer, insurer and terminal operator by October 31. He argues the 2022 Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act bars the cargo regardless of Treasury's General License 135, which authorizes Russian diesel transactions through April 7, 2027. A bipartisan group of lawmakers has warned banks — including Goldman Sachs — and port authorities in Houston, Corpus Christi, Beaumont and New York/New Jersey of liability exposure.

Two further tankers, the Leruo and the Talisman, are carrying Russian diesel toward the U.S.; Kpler puts the three cargoes at 924,000 barrels. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said a fourth was expected to sail on October 28. With no declared port and banks and terminals warned away, the cargo could be redirected to Cuba, which ran out of diesel and fuel oil in May.
sections.whyItMatters: A presidential license that banks and ports refuse to honor is not a policy — it is a legal dispute. The diesel deal's real test is not whether tankers sail but whether anyone onshore will take delivery.

sections.heading: Tanker Windfalls and the Chinese Refinery Pivot to Africa and Brazil
sections.body:
Saudi shipping giant Bahri reported third-quarter net profit of $1.36 billion, ten times the $137 million booked a year earlier and up 85% on the second quarter, driven by its Bahri Oil unit. The company attributed the surge to record tanker rates as Hormuz disruption and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman tie up VLCCs for weeks.

Those same rates are re-routing Chinese crude sourcing. With freight easing about $10 per barrel from early-October records, Chinese refiners bought West African and Brazilian grades at premiums of up to $20 per barrel over ICE Brent for December delivery — Equatorial Guinea's Ceiba, Angola's Saturno and Brazil's Mero — according to Bloomberg. Competition with India has pushed up Russia's ESPO grade, and Iranian barrels have disappeared from the teapot refiner feedstock pool.

UBS, meanwhile, raised its Brent forecast for the second time this month to $110 for end-2026 and lifted its 2027 curve to $95 (March), $90 (June) and $85 (September), citing VLCC rates from the Middle East to China at $30-40 per barrel versus $1-3 over the past decade.
sections.whyItMatters: Freight is now doing the work sanctions and war used to do: it is deciding which barrels reach which refineries. Bahri's profit is the cleanest measure of how much value the crisis is transferring from cargo owners to shipowners.

sections.heading: Rare Earths: Washington's 2027 Deadline Meets a 300-Tonne Domestic Base
sections.body:
As the Pentagon's January 1, 2027 sourcing rules approach — designed to remove Chinese-origin rare earth magnets from defense procurement — the civilian gap remains enormous. Reuters reported the U.S. consumed about 48,000 tonnes of rare earth permanent magnets in 2025 but produced only about 300 tonnes domestically.

The IEA estimates a complete Chinese cutoff could put roughly $6.5 trillion of downstream industrial production outside China at risk, while the Department of War's own procurement accounts for less than 0.1% of global rare earth demand, according to the GAO. China has further tightened controls by restricting the movement of individuals with sensitive technical knowledge, per Oilprice.com.
sections.whyItMatters: The defense deadline will be met on paper and missed in substance. The binding constraint is separation and metallization capacity outside China, which is measured in years, not in procurement rules.

bottomLine: Gas is now the sharper edge of this war than crude. QatarEnergy's decision to extend force majeure to year-end takes the world's largest LNG exporter effectively out of Europe's second consecutive winter and out of South Asia's power mix entirely, with TTF back at 2022 levels and Pakistan borrowing a billion dollars to keep the lights on. Oil markets, by contrast, have adapted — Saudi Arabia and Iran are both finding routes, Chinese refiners are pivoting to African and Brazilian crude, and shipowners like Bahri are capturing the difference. The risks that remain are binary: an Iranian answer to Qatar's draft this week, and a possible renewed U.S. campaign after November 3 that Gulf capitals have already been told to prepare for. If either breaks badly, the LNG shortfall is the transmission channel that reaches households first.
sources: Oilprice.com, Reuters, Bloomberg, Kpler, ICIS, UANI, Fars News Agency via Iran International, Wall Street Journal via The National, Jerusalem Post, Edison, Petrobangla, Tribune Pakistan, Wood Mackenzie, UBS, IEA, GAO, IMF, Saudi Exchange (Bahri filing)
